Sexual maturation in this species occurs when individuals reach a total length of about 28 centimeters [Lp = about 28 centimeters], a threshold that appears to be reached after several years of slow growth in the cold, food-limited waters of the Southern Ocean. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from their demersal eggs at a remarkably early developmental stage, with the age at hatch documented at 50.5 days [ab = 50.5 days] when incubated at a stable temperature of 4.9 °C [T = 4.9 °C]. This protracted incubation period, typical of many deep-water teleosts, reflects the retarded metabolic rates imposed by the frigid thermal environment. This substantial body mass, combined with an exceptionally long life span estimated at 140 years [am = 140 years] under the prevailing deep-sea temperature regime of 4.9 °C [T = 4.9 °C], positions this species among the more extreme examples of slow life-history strategies observed in teleost fishes. The trade-off between investment in a few large, yolk-rich eggs and the production of numerous small pelagic eggs is heavily skewed toward the latter strategy in this species, ensuring broad spatial dispersal despite the high mortality rates of early life stages.

This protracted juvenile phase is a key demographic bottleneck, making the species particularly sensitive to fluctuations in food availability and oceanographic conditions that affect growth rates.
